It is true, then, to say with regard to their mixture that the aristolochia is more in substance and in quality and in activity, and prevails over the others. One might say this very same thing also in the case of the bath-house, when it has within it not only the well-tempered air but has taken on in addition something of smoke and of vapour. For of these, sometimes the smoke can be more, sometimes the vapour, just as also the air of the bath-house that is in accordance with nature. But we say 'simply' not of what is more by the excess of its substance, with which it is necessary that the quality and the activity deriving from it also increase together. Let it be supposed, at any rate, that the substance of the smoke is more than that of the other two; you will then rightly say that the quality of the smoke too is more than the quality of the others, and the activity as well.

It is agreed, however, that a quality does not become 'more' than a quality, but 'more intense', just as also 'fainter', not 'less', though such a use of the words is extremely common throughout the whole book and in all the arts. And why need one mention the others, when we have a manifest witness to the argument in the fevers themselves, which everyone says every day have become greater or less than one another, and at times that someone is feverish less or more, and that this man's fever is the same yesterday or today? With it thus laid down that the 'more' in respect of quality is so spoken of, it is no wonder, in a bath-house in which the substance of smoke is greater, to say that the quality too has become more, and the activity: 'strong' and 'more intense', if we are naming properly; 'greater' and 'more', if by misuse. For the smoke will evidently bite the eyes to the degree that it increases also in substance; so that, since the qualities proper to the substances and the activities always increase together with the substances, one might truly say that in such a bath-house the smoke is greatest.

For one heat is kindled from the blood, another from the phlegm, another from the yellow or the black bile.
